solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Old European coin originally accepted in Tube

explanation.surface: A numismatist describes an old coin found, or accepted as fare, on the London Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tube' tempts you towards the London Underground; here it is just a pipe, DUCT, which takes the A inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The ducat was a gold or silver coin used across Europe from the Middle Ages.

clue.text: Detective wickedly arresting attorney in supercilious way

explanation.surface: A crooked detective looks down his nose while arresting a lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wickedly' looks like an adverb on the detective; it becomes a whole word of wordplay. DA is the American district attorney, a public prosecutor.
explanation.definitionFit: To act disdainfully is to act in a supercilious, scornful way.

clue.text: Oil producer caught last of audience leaving Tosca, perhaps

blocks.clueFragment: last of audience leaving Tosca, perhaps
blocks.note: OPERA, of which Tosca is one, loses E, the last letter of audience

explanation.surface: An audience member slips out of a performance of Puccini's Tosca.
explanation.walkthrough: Tosca is Puccini's opera, so 'Tosca, perhaps' is OPERA; take out the E and put C in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Copra is dried coconut kernel, pressed to produce coconut oil.

clue.text: Club treasurer deprived of filling meal without starter

explanation.surface: A club's treasurer goes hungry at a lunch served with no first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' reads as a society with a treasurer; it is the policeman's weapon. 'Filling' and 'starter' keep up the meal picture while doing the trimming.
explanation.definitionFit: A truncheon is a short thick club, as carried by police.

clue.text: The old ship’s officer engaging satisfactory working companion

blocks.note: a mate is a ship's officer

explanation.surface: An old-time ship's officer hires a decent hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old' is not an adjective on the ship: it is the archaic spelling of 'the', with the Y standing for the old letter thorn.
explanation.definitionFit: A yokemate is one yoked with another, so a fellow worker or partner.

clue.text: Food tent includes game counter

blocks.note: a yurt is a round felt tent of Central Asia

explanation.surface: A food tent at a fair has a counter for a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counter' looks like a shop counter in the tent or a game piece; it is the reversal instruction for GO.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by broad category: yogurt, milk fermented by bacteria, is one of countless things that count as food.

clue.text: Tree creature in Kojak manipulated for all to see?

indicators.note: the letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: U = universal film certificate, suitable for all audiences

explanation.surface: A creature turns up on the TV detective show Kojak, twisted into view for the whole audience.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film rating meaning anyone may watch, so 'for all to see' is U, added to the anagram. Kojak was a 1970s US police drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The kinkajou is a tree-dwelling mammal of Central and South American rainforests.

clue.text: Merriment rare at first in US university hospital

blocks.note: H = hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Laughter is seldom heard in an American university hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: R sits inside MIT, then H follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Mirth is merriment, laughter and good cheer.

clue.text: One-time militia’s aim reportedly disallowed

indicators.note: the next word is given by its sound

blocks.note: to train a gun is to aim it

explanation.surface: A news report says an old militia's objective has been outlawed.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is part of the surface, not the answer. 'Aim' is the verb: you train a weapon on a target.
explanation.definitionFit: Trainbands were citizen militias in England from the 16th to 18th centuries.

clue.text: Elderly person exercising parentage in USA

indicators.note: the letters are worked out, put through their paces

explanation.surface: An old American is using the rights of a parent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as a link but is part of the fodder, giving the I and N the anagram needs.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin septuageni, 'seventy each': someone aged seventy to seventy-nine is fairly called elderly.

clue.text: Wife supporting more benevolent prodigies?

blocks.note: in a down entry, something under holds up what is above

explanation.surface: A wife backs up nicer children who show special promise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporting' reads as a verb; it is simply UNDER. The question mark flags that the answer is German, the plural of wunderkind.
explanation.definitionFit: Wunderkinder, 'wonder children', are child prodigies.

clue.text: A jarring song dismissing old American tree

blocks.note: raucous = harsh, jarring on the ear
an aria is an operatic song

explanation.surface: A harsh-sounding song leaves out an old American tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dismissing old American' is the deletion, stripping O and US from RAUCOUS; 'American' is not a definition of the tree. Araucaria was also the pen name of the great Guardian setter John Graham.
explanation.definitionFit: Araucaria is the genus of trees that includes the monkey puzzle.

clue.text: Believer helping to build church in Dublin

indicators.note: the words together contain, and so help make up, the answer

explanation.surface: A person of faith helps build a church in the Irish capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The church in Dublin suggests a Christian; the believer is of another faith altogether.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a follower of the Hindu faith is one kind of religious believer.

clue.text: Relative’s narrow escape originally? That was a close shave!

indicators.note: take the first letter of each word

blocks.note: phew! is what you say after a close shave

explanation.surface: A relative has a near miss and exhales in relief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relative's' is 'Relative is': the 's joins definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: your brother's or sister's son is one of your relatives.

clue.text: Puller of strings beginning to push drug plugged by supporter on course

blocks.note: an upper is a stimulant drug
on a golf course a tee holds up the ball

explanation.surface: A string-puller starts pushing drugs, backed by someone at the racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puller of strings' suggests a behind-the-scenes fixer; it is literal. 'Supporter on course' is golf, not a racegoer.
explanation.definitionFit: A puppeteer works a marionette by pulling its strings.

clue.text: Female slave 007 caused to be heard

indicators.note: the word before is given by its sound

explanation.surface: James Bond forces a woman in bondage to be listened to.
explanation.walkthrough: BOND is spelt, only 'caused' is sounded.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word: a maid held in bondage, bound to serve without pay, was a slave girl.

clue.text: Return of traditional management is target in sport

indicators.note: TRAD comes back the other way

blocks.note: the board is a company's management

explanation.surface: A company brings back old-fashioned management as its sporting goal.
explanation.walkthrough: Only TRAD turns round; BOARD reads forwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The ringed board that players throw darts at is what they aim for, so the target of the pub sport.

clue.text: Concur with writer about shade

explanation.surface: Agree with an author on the matter of a colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' only links; the writer is the pen, not the author.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the yellowish green of garden peas is one shade, or colour.

clue.text: On the loose in Berlin and consuming pasta

indicators.note: to consume is to eat, taking something inside

explanation.surface: Someone is out and about in Berlin, eating pasta.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Berlin' reads as the setting; it tells you to put 'and' into German.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal unpenned is let out of its pen, so free and on the loose.

clue.text: Merchant bringing socialist realism to the West?

indicators.note: an across entry read towards the west runs right to left

blocks.note: socialist realism is a style of art

explanation.surface: A businessman imports Soviet-style propaganda art to Western galleries.
explanation.walkthrough: Socialist realism is the Soviet art style, so RED ART; reversed it gives TRADER. The question mark admits 'realism' is only loosely ART.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a merchant makes a living by buying and selling goods, which is what trading is.

clue.text: Young singer, extremely bashful, overwhelmed by elder, maybe

indicators.note: to be overwhelmed is to be engulfed, so the letters end up swallowed inside the tree

explanation.surface: A shy young chorister is overawed by an older person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elder' reads as an older person, fitting the young singer; it is the elder tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A treble is a boy soprano in a choir.

clue.text: City is in prime position, we’re told

indicators.note: what we hear, not what is written

blocks.note: one who leads is in first place

explanation.surface: A city is said to be top of the table.
explanation.walkthrough: Leeds is a large city in Yorkshire, northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Leeds, in West Yorkshire, is one of England's largest cities.

clue.text: Completely filled three empty blue boxes

indicators.note: as a verb, to box is to put in a box

explanation.surface: Someone completely filled three unused blue boxes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxes' is the verb, SAD boxing TE; 'filled' in the surface goes with the boxes, but belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: after a big meal your appetite is fully satisfied, with no room left for more.

clue.text: Soldier eating a coarse type of biscuit

indicators.note: what is eaten ends up inside the eater

blocks.note: a GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A soldier munches on a rough army biscuit.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, the Garibaldi biscuit is named after an Italian soldier. It is a flat British biscuit layered with currants.
explanation.definitionFit: A garibaldi is a type of biscuit with a layer of squashed currants.

clue.text: Row over new bedding, for example

explanation.surface: A quarrel breaks out over new sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' rhymes with 'cow' in the surface, a quarrel; it is a line. In a down entry LINE sits over N.
explanation.definitionFit: Bed sheets and pillowcases are linen, so bedding is one example.

clue.text: Forgetful old man knocked out crossing end of drive

blocks.note: to brain someone is to knock them out with a blow to the head

explanation.surface: An absent-minded old man is flattened as he crosses the end of a driveway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked out' reads as describing the old man's state; it is the wordplay's final piece, and 'old man' is British slang for father.
explanation.definitionFit: Featherbrained means scatterbrained or silly, so apt to forget.

clue.text: Caution coppers guarding duke after game

explanation.surface: Police officers warn a duke as they protect him after a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' are police in the surface; here they are coins, and PENCE is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: acting with care and forethought to avoid risk is both prudent and cautious.

clue.text: One who gives out refreshments initially by river?

indicators.note: take the first letter of each word

blocks.note: the Don, a river in Yorkshire, Scotland and Russia

explanation.surface: A riverside tea stall worker hands out refreshments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One who gives out refreshments' reads as a single phrase; the definition stops at 'gives', and 'out' gives only its O. 'By' puts OR beside DON.
explanation.definitionFit: A donor is one who gives, especially money, blood or organs.
